title: The 10 Best Corded Random Orbital Sanders
subtitle: Wired 5-inch random orbit sanders ranked from live Amazon data — swirl-free finishes for the least money, no battery to run down.
intro: A random orbital sander spins and orbits its pad at the same time, so it smooths wood and metal without leaving the swirl marks a fixed rotary sander does. Corded models give you steady power for long sessions and cost far less than a cordless tool plus its battery, which is why they still lead the category. This list covers 5-inch sanders from budget kits under $30 to pro tools, sorted by what varies most: variable speed, how they collect dust, and whether they ship ready to sand.

products.name: DEWALT Orbital Sander Kit, 5 inch, 3 Amp, Corded, 12,000 OPM (DWE6421K)
products.verdict: The everyday pick for most people. The 3-amp motor runs a fixed 12,000 OPM, the short body gets you close to the work, and the dust port clicks onto a DEWALT vac or any 1-1/4" shop-vac hose for real dust control. Ships as a kit with a dust bag and a carrying bag, and carries a 3-year warranty.
pros: 5,587 reviews at 4.7 stars
Dust port fits DEWALT collectors and 1-1/4" shop-vac hoses
3-year warranty and a carrying bag included
cons: Single speed — no dial for delicate finishing
The cloth dust bag fills fast and passes fine dust

products.name: SKIL 5" Random Orbital Sander with Cyclonic Dust Box & 3pc Sanding Sheet (SR211601)
products.verdict: The value pick, and the best-selling random orbital sander on Amazon at 6,000+ a month. Under $40 gets you variable speed and a clear cyclonic dust box that snaps off to empty, plus three sanding sheets to start. A lot of tool for the money, and the reason it's the category's #1 seller.

products.name: DEWALT Random Orbit Sander, Variable Speed, 5-Inch (DWE6423)
products.verdict: The variable-speed version of the DWE6421 above, and worth the extra money if you sand a range of materials. The dial runs 8,000 to 12,000 OPM, so you can slow down for veneer, paint, or finishing and open it up for stock removal. Same DEWALT vac port and 3-year warranty.

products.name: BOSCH ROS20VSC Palm Sander, Variable Speed Random Orbital Sander with Dust Canister & Carrying Bag
products.verdict: The most feature-complete sander here. Variable speed, a pad-dampening system that fights swirl marks on lift-off, and a twist-off dust canister with a microfilter that traps particles down to half a micron. Comes with the canister, a vacuum adapter, and a carrying bag, so it does everything out of the box.

It's the highest-rated sander on the list at 4.8 stars, with the widest speed range here (4,000 to 12,000 OPM), a rubberized palm grip that kills vibration, and a hard case. You pay for it, but Makita build quality is why it lasts.

avoid.name: ZFE Random Orbital Sander 5" & 6" Pneumatic Palm Sander
avoid.flag: Air-powered — needs a compressor, not a wall outlet
avoid.verdict: This isn't an electric sander. It's a pneumatic (air) tool that does nothing on its own — it needs an air compressor most buyers don't have, yet it sits in the results right beside plug-in sanders. If you want to plug in and sand, any of the corded tools above is the right buy.
reasons: Its power source is pneumatic: it runs on compressed air, not electricity, and has no cord or plug. It won't turn on without an air compressor, which is not included and typically costs $100 to $300 more than the sander.

The listing buries that. It's titled simply "Random Orbital Sander," ranks alongside corded electric sanders, and even lists a "1 A" amperage and a "10,000 rpm" spec — figures that make no sense for an air tool and make it easy to mistake for an electric one.

A palm air sander like this needs a steady 5 to 7 CFM at 90 PSI to run continuously. Many small pancake and hot-dog home compressors can't sustain that, so even a buyer who owns one may find the tool starves and slows under load.
It's a 5"/6" combo that needs backing-plate swaps, and 6" discs are less common and pricier than the 5" hook-and-loop discs every electric sander above uses.

buyers_guide.a: The pad spins in a circle and orbits off-center at the same time, so it never traces the same path twice. That random motion is what stops it from leaving the circular swirl marks a fixed rotary sander leaves, which is why it's the go-to for finishing wood before paint or stain.

Variable speed lets you slow the pad down for delicate work like veneer, paint prep, or polishing, where full speed can burn or gouge, and speed it up for fast stock removal. If you only sand bare wood, a single-speed tool like the DEWALT DWE6421K or BLACK+DECKER is fine. For mixed materials, pay for the dial.

buyers_guide.q: Dust bag, canister, or shop vac?
buyers_guide.a: A cloth dust bag is convenient but fills fast and lets fine dust through. A cyclonic box or twist-off canister (SKIL, Bosch) is tidier and shows the fill level. The cleanest option is a tool with a vacuum port, like the DEWALT, CRAFTSMAN, or Metabo HPT picks, hooked to a shop vac — it collects the most and keeps the air clearer.

Yes. Five-inch hook-and-loop discs are the most common and cheapest sandpaper you can buy, and every tool on this list uses them. Match the disc's hole pattern (usually 8 holes) to the pad so the dust extraction lines up.

A corded sander gives constant power for long sanding sessions and costs much less, since there's no battery to buy. Cordless only makes sense if you need to sand where a cord can't reach or you're already invested in a battery platform.

buyers_guide.q: What do the OPM numbers mean?
buyers_guide.a: OPM is orbits per minute — how fast the pad moves. Higher OPM removes material faster; most 5-inch sanders top out around 12,000 to 13,000 OPM. On a variable-speed tool, the low end matters just as much: it's what lets you dial back for a fine finish.
